after: ## A key distinction: committing crime versus being recorded
alt: A narrowing funnel from everyone who commits crime, to those caught, recorded by police and convicted. Official statistics measure the lower stages. Below, three reasons a group can appear more often: it offends more, it is policed more, or both.
caption: Official statistics show who is caught and recorded, not simply who offends.

alt: Two panels. Explanations of more working-class offending: Merton’s blocked opportunities, Albert Cohen’s status frustration and material deprivation. Explanations of how recording skews the pattern: interactionist labelling by police, and Marxist arguments that white collar and corporate crime are under-represented.
caption: Some explanations say the working class offend more; others say they are simply recorded more.

alt: Five steps: working-class boys share mainstream success goals; educational failure and poor job prospects block them; they suffer status frustration; they join a delinquent subculture valuing stealing, vandalism and truancy; success in it brings prestige. Below, a strength and a criticism.
caption: For Albert Cohen, the subculture gives blocked boys another way to win status.

alt: Three cards. Heidensohn: patriarchal societies control women more at home, in public and at work. Socialisation: boys are encouraged to take risks, girls to be careful. Pollak’s chivalry thesis: the justice system treats women more leniently, though critics say women who break gender norms are treated more harshly.
caption: Two explanations are about offending; the chivalry thesis is about recording.

alt: Carlen interviewed 39 convicted women and used control theory. In the class deal women give wage labour for consumer goods; in the gender deal they give love and domestic labour for psychological and material rewards from a male breadwinner. When the rewards are unavailable, through poverty, unemployment, abuse or care, crime becomes a viable alternative.
caption: When the class and gender deals fail, crime becomes a rational choice.

alt: Left: some minority groups, particularly Black people, are over-represented in stop and search, arrest and prison; explanations are discrimination and labelling (the Macpherson Report), deprivation and media stereotypes. Right: a schematic curve of recorded offending peaking in the late teens and early twenties, with reasons such as visibility, peer pressure and having less to lose.
caption: For ethnicity and age, ask whether the pattern reflects offending, policing, or both.

alt: A chain: exaggerated reporting turns a group into folk devils, raising public concern and police attention, which leads to more recorded deviance, called deviancy amplification. Below, a reminder not to confuse Albert Cohen, on delinquent subcultures, with Stanley Cohen, on moral panics.
caption: Exaggerated media coverage can create the very rise in deviance it reports.
